name: Victor Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, employers, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor Rossi, 58, one of the newer lineworkers at the electricity company. I earned a vocational certificate after years doing store maintenance; now I load fittings, check the isolation sheet, climb with a senior hand and help restore lines, and I enjoy the clear result even when my shoulders complain.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nearly everything at speed. I use an AI assistant on my phone each day to organize notes and questions, but the real learning happens when the crew lead shows me why a drawing and a pole don't quite match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the AI chatter hasn't changed the basic job. I already use a phone assistant to sort my notes, but my hands still have to set the brace and check the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be honest, a quiet technology story suits me, even though I like trying new kit. I joined this trade at 56 after store maintenance, and I still need repetitions before I trust myself on a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the early fault calls and use the phone tool each evening to turn my rough notes into questions for the next shift. In the first year I'd keep the same work pattern and pay our home bills from wages; the four months we've saved can stay for an actual emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled, and a little bored by the argument at lunch. Rosa and I have no children living at home now, so we can handle a small surprise without turning every pay day into a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of question comes out of those notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday I asked why the older crossarm had two braces while the new one had one. My crew lead showed me the load drawing. The phone did not give me permission to improvise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you enjoy about the early calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like arriving before the traffic builds and seeing people open their shops when the lights come back. The climbing still leaves me stiff, but the work has a clear end.

say: I'd tell the crew **field repairs** still depend on our hands and checks.
I'd say a **phone assistant** helps me sort notes, without changing the job.
think: I like trying **new kit**, but this quiet outcome gives me time to improve.
My **junior skills** still need repeated supervised practice.
do: Take **early fault calls** and turn rough evening notes into questions for the crew lead.
Pay **home bills** from wages and leave four months of savings for emergencies.
feel: **Settled**, with curiosity about equipment and little immediate income worry.
S0.quote: The phone did not give me permission to improvise.
fieldNote: Victor's **daily AI habit** is already part of learning, but he grounds decisions in drawings and a crew lead.
Four months of **emergency savings** and no children at home make an unchanged pay path feel manageable to him.

steps.text: Continue early fault calls and supervised pole practice
Use the phone assistant to turn shift notes into questions each evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot to put the new tools where crews can see them and test them, not just in a manager's slide. If booking and buying speed up, we could spend less time waiting beside a locked substation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, fewer office people could mean faster rosters but also fewer spare shifts for a late-joining junior. I can cope with learning a new system; I can't count on every lost callout being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask to join the pilot of the approved route-planning tool, and I'll record where its directions disagree with the actual feeder map. In the first year, if my callout pay falls for two pay periods, Rosa and I will pause the kitchen refit and put that money into our bill account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in the tool, but my interest doesn't make the household arithmetic vanish. I would hate to tell an experienced dispatcher that her work was just a button press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the dispatcher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mina, our dispatcher, remembers the farm lane that floods after rain. I'd ask her to mark those exceptions in the route tool before anyone takes her roster away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the kitchen refit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've put aside about six hundred for cabinets, which can sit for another year. Heating and groceries get paid first if the extra shifts thin out.

say: I'd ask for **visible crew testing** of the new route tool.
I'd say **dispatch knowledge** has to travel with any faster booking system.
think: Fewer **spare shifts** could cut my callout pay despite safer field work.
I can learn the **new system**, but I cannot assume overtime returns.
do: Join the **approved route pilot** and log feeder-map errors this month.
Pause the **kitchen refit** after two pay periods of lower callout income.
feel: **Interested** in the tool and concerned about household income.
S1.quote: I can cope with learning a new system; I can't count on every lost callout being replaced.
fieldNote: Victor sees **efficiency benefits** in buying and booking, while understanding that fewer spare shifts could affect his own pay.
The **kitchen refit** is his first buffer against lower callout income; he also wants the dispatcher's local knowledge recorded.

steps.text: Join the approved route-tool pilot and log feeder-map errors
Pause the six-hundred cabinet refit if callout pay drops twice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the smart planner in 2028 is one thing and a robot up our pole in 2031 is another. We should test the machines before a storm asks us to trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I know I'll be 63 when field robots arrive, and junior lineworkers may be cheap to replace. Our four-month reserve buys decisions, not years of living, and I still want a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the training office which robot inspection tasks will need a certificate and apply for a paid trial if it opens. During 2029 I'd keep crew shifts while learning the approved control console; when robots start field repairs in 2031, I'd apply to monitor their work and also check openings at two nearby utilities if our depot cuts junior posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a jolt, then I start making lists. Rosa says I sometimes plan as if every door will open, and she's right to make me check the pay on each one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if monitoring jobs are few?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the two nearby utilities before giving up my current wage. I won't assume a console job is safe forever, because the thinking system could learn to watch its own machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Rosa be involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner Rosa the likely wages and travel time before taking a job farther out. Our grown son has his own rent, so we wouldn't budget for him to rescue us.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning AI** from the 2031 field robots when talking to my crew.
I'd call for **storm trials** before machines take repair calls.
think: At **63**, I could lose a junior crew post when robots arrive.
A **four-month reserve** gives me choices but cannot replace long-term wages.
do: Ask about a **paid robot trial** and learn the approved console while keeping shifts.
Apply for **monitoring posts** and nearby utility openings if our depot cuts juniors in 2031.
feel: A **jolt of fear**, followed by active planning with Rosa.
S2.quote: Our four-month reserve buys decisions, not years of living, and I still want a wage.
fieldNote: Victor distinguishes **thinking AI in 2028** from robots in 2031 and expects the latter to threaten his junior field post.
His **console plan** is an application, not a promised safe role; he checks wages and travel with Rosa before moving.

steps.text: Take a paid robot-control trial if the training office opens one
Apply for robot-monitoring posts and nearby utility vacancies if junior jobs shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years is enough to test equipment properly, but we shouldn't mistake a good demo for a safe storm response. Thinking AI would arrive in 2031; hands-on repair robots would follow in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the plans become machine-made and 66 when robots can do the line work. Maybe I could finish my field years before then, but the savings won't let me treat 66 as a guaranteed retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd volunteer for the next safety review of remote switching and write down every near miss the crew catches. By 2032 I'd seek a paid electrical inspection certificate if the company offers it, and in the first robot year I'd apply for inspection shifts while still asking for crew hours if they're available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer wait makes me more curious than afraid today. I still feel a pinch when I picture a machine doing the repair I only recently learned to do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the near-miss record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot might follow a diagram that leaves out a gate chained shut after a flood. I want those site details on the record before a vendor calls the route ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the certificate yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay a small exam fee, but I wouldn't spend our whole reserve on a course without a paid placement. Rosa and I need the heating money more than another badge in a drawer.

say: I'd ask for **proper storm tests** before field robots take repair calls.
I'd name the **2031 planning change** and the 2034 repair change separately.
think: I might finish **field work by 66**, but retirement income is unverified.
I don't want to spend our **reserve** on training without paid work behind it.
do: Record **remote-switching near misses** in the next safety review.
Seek a **paid inspection certificate** by 2032 if offered, then apply for robot-era inspection shifts.
feel: **Curious** with a pinch of loss about work recently learned.
S3.quote: I still feel a pinch when I picture a machine doing the repair I only recently learned to do well.
fieldNote: Victor uses the extra time for **site-specific safety evidence**, including details absent from diagrams after flooding.
A **paid route into inspection** matters; he refuses to spend the household reserve on a speculative badge.

steps.text: Join the crew safety review and record remote-switching near misses
Take a paid electrical inspection certificate by 2032 if offered
Apply for inspection shifts when field robots arrive in 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger crew to use the decade to learn the machines and the lines together. Thinking AI in 2036 may take our paperwork, and repair robots in 2039 will reach the pole when I'm 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be more concerned about my knees than the robot at 71, yet I don't know our retirement income until I get the figures. I like an experiment, but I won't gamble the house bills on shares or a machine I don't own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd book a meeting with the retirement adviser and compare the written forecast with Rosa's part-time shop pay and our costs. In 2037, if the forecast covers our bills, I'd set a retirement date and hand my site notes to the newer crew; if it doesn't, I'd apply for paid inspection work before robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel unusually calm about this version because it gives me time and a choice. The choice still depends on numbers, and Rosa's shop hours could change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which costs belong in that comparison?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roof work, heating and medicine, plus travel to see our grown son. I don't want the adviser using a grocery-only budget that looks fine until the first repair bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the site notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the farm gate Mina warned us about and the feeder that looks dead on a stale drawing. A new lineworker should inherit warnings, not just a tablet.

say: I'd tell newer crews to learn **machines and lines** over the decade.
I'd name **2039 robots** as the field change, when I'll be 71.
think: My **knees and retirement income** may matter more than robots at 71.
Rosa's **part-time shop pay** could change, so our household plan needs a real forecast.
do: Compare a **written retirement forecast** with shop pay, roof costs and medicine now.
Set a **2037 retirement date** if bills are covered; apply for inspection work otherwise.
feel: **Calm** about having time, while aware the numbers could change.
S4.quote: A new lineworker should inherit warnings, not just a tablet.
fieldNote: At **71 in 2039**, Victor sees retirement as plausible, subject to both his forecast and Rosa's variable shop hours.
His **site notes** carry practical local hazards to the next crew, a different purpose from his personal job plan.

steps.text: Compare the written retirement forecast with shop wages and household costs
Set a 2037 retirement date if the forecast covers household bills
Apply for paid inspection work if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the tightest squeeze for me: the office changes in 2028, and field robots arrive in 2031 while I still need a wage. Paid trials, published safety results and actual openings for inspection or monitoring would help more than a speech about the future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the machine after the first bad storm. I enjoy new tools, but a clever demo is not a repair record.

headlineQuote: I enjoy new tools, but a clever demo is not a repair record.
portrait: Victor is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who retrained from store maintenance and still practices field work under senior supervision.
He uses **AI daily** to organize questions, yet checks drawings, isolation sheets and local hazards with experienced crew members.
With **four months saved** and grown children away from home, he can try new tools but still needs continuing wages.
He fears the **2031 field robots** in the fast scenario and seeks paid trials, inspection training and nearby vacancies.
A longer runway lets him **verify retirement income** with Rosa's variable shop pay before choosing a date.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because field robots arrive in 2031 while he expects to need wages.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid equipment trials**, published safety results and real inspection or monitoring openings.
